query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In the high-temperature regime (above ~500 °C), wear resistance of a thin FeNiCrCoCu coating on steel is chiefly governed by the formation and stability of a protective oxide scale. Inducing a stable oxide layer via a controlled pre-oxidation step will significantly reduce abrasive and adhesive wear under elevated-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin coating on a conventional steel substrate, unheated prior to wear testing.
generation.intervention: Mild pre-oxidation at ~600 °C in air to form an initial oxide scale on the as-deposited coating, followed by the same high-temperature sliding wear tests used for the baseline.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests in the 25–900 °C range under 10–30 N normal load, measuring friction and wear track depth while monitoring oxide evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: Stable, adherent oxide layer that mitigates direct metal–metal asperity contact and reduces oxidation-driven adhesion at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: The pre-oxidation step promotes oxide scale formation on the coating. This stable oxide acts as a barrier against severe metal-on-metal contact, decreasing friction, lessening oxidative and adhesive wear, and improving surface integrity at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the un-oxidized baseline, the pre-oxidized FeNiCrCoCu coating will show measurably lower friction coefficients and wear rates (e.g., up to ~20–30% reduction in track depth) above ~500 °C, with minimal oxide spallation.
generation.baseline: Un-oxidized as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating subject to the same sliding wear tests, expected to exhibit higher friction and more severe wear at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Temperature range from ambient to ~900 °C and normal loads up to 30 N. If tested beyond these extremes, the oxide scale may spall or degrade, diminishing the protective effect.
generation.uncertainty: While prior results on related multicomponent coatings suggest beneficial oxide formation, direct confirmation of this mechanism for FeNiCrCoCu over the full 25–900 °C range is lacking and must be experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu-coated steel samples: (1) as-deposited control; (2) pre-oxidized for a fixed duration at ~600 °C in air. Conduct identical pin-on-disk or reciprocating sliding tests at temperatures from 25 °C to 900 °C under 10–30 N loads. Compare friction coefficients, wear track depths, and oxide spallation via optical and electron microscopy.
measurements: Coefficient of friction over time and temperature
Post-test wear volume and wear track depth
Surface characterization and oxide layer thickness/chemical composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit reduced wear rates or friction compared to the baseline, and if no stable oxide scale is observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. decision.trend: Recent work on multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) for wear applications at elevated temperatures has focused on improving tribological performance by leveraging the formation of protective oxide scales. In particular, AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 coatings showed diminished wear at 800–900°C linked to in situ spinel oxide formation. Similarly, nanocrystalline refractory HEA films were developed to enhance mechanical and tribological performance up to moderate temperatures, with emphasis on hard, thermally stable surfaces. However, these studies largely focused on specific compositions or partial temperature ranges, leaving open the broader question of how to control high-temperature wear across a wide operating regime in thin, expensive MPEA coatings such as FeNiCrCoCu.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear which mechanistic pathway dominates high-temperature wear behavior in FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings, particularly the roles of in situ oxide scale formation, microstructural evolution, and substrate interactions over a broad thermal and loading range.
decision.lever: In a baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating (as-deposited), implement a mild pre-oxidation treatment at ~600°C in air to intentionally form a thin, stable oxide layer prior to high-temperature sliding wear tests in the 25–900°C range under 10–30 N normal load, tracking oxide evolution in situ if possible.
decision.why: Based on evidence from AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 coatings that a robust oxide scale can significantly reduce wear at elevated temperature, the most direct testable hypothesis is that FeNiCrCoCu forms a protective oxide layer under specific pre-oxidation conditions, thereby reducing adhesive and abrasive wear above ~500°C. If the scale is protective, we expect decreased friction coefficients, shallower wear tracks, and limited oxide spallation, confirming the oxide-based wear resistance mechanism. A null or adverse change in wear behavior, or the absence of stable oxide coverage, would falsify this mechanism.
